opus-5.5.text:
That's one of my favorite problems, because it sits right where philosophy and neuroscience meet. There's a famous thought experiment from the philosopher Quine. You're a linguist with a tribe whose language you don't know. A rabbit runs by, someone points and says "gavagai." You write down "gavagai means rabbit." But how do you actually know? It could mean "undetached rabbit parts," or "dinner," or "look, something moving," or "the spirit of the forest is visiting." Every time you test it, the rabbit is there, so all of those interpretations fit the evidence equally well. Logically, you can never fully pin it down.

What I find fascinating as a neuroscientist is that we still manage it. Babies do this all the time. Nobody hands a one-year-old a dictionary, and yet they converge on meaning. So the brain must be bringing assumptions to the table, priors, that cut down the space of possibilities. We tend to assume a word refers to a whole object rather than its parts. We assume a new word refers to something we don't already have a name for. And most importantly, we follow attention. If you point and you're looking at the rabbit with excitement, I assume you care about the thing, not the grass behind it.

So interpretation without a shared language isn't really about the word. It's about building a model of the other mind. You're asking, "What is this person paying attention to, and what do they want me to notice?" That's a much older system in the brain than language. And the implication is a bit humbling: even when we do share a language, you and I right now, I never actually know exactly what you mean. I'm running the same guessing game, with better priors. Communication is less transferring information and more two brains trying to align themselves closely enough that the guess is good enough.

r001.rationale: It describes the rabbit-and-“gavagai” example and explains that alternatives like “undetached rabbit parts,” “dinner,” or “something moving” fit the evidence, so “rabbit” is not uniquely established.

fable-5.1.text:
So, this is actually one of my favorite problems, because it's where my two worlds collide. I'm a neuroscientist, but before that I was a hacker, and this is really a decryption problem.

Think about it this way. If someone says a word to you and you don't speak their language, the sound itself carries almost nothing. "Table" means nothing in the acoustic signal. The meaning isn't in the word. The meaning is in everything around the word.

So what does my brain do? It starts using context as a key. Where are they pointing? What's their face doing? What happened right before they said it, and what happens right after? If they say the word and then hand me a cup, my brain starts building a hypothesis. Maybe the word is "cup," maybe it's "drink," maybe it's "take," maybe it's "here." And I hold all those options alive at the same time, and each new instance kills some of them off. That's exactly how you break a code. You look for repetitions, you look for correlations with the environment, and you let the structure reveal itself.

What's beautiful is that we have evidence the brain does this constantly, even with people who share our language. When I record from neurons in patients, we can see that the same word activates different patterns depending on who's speaking, what the tone is, what was said earlier. The brain never really trusts the word alone. It's always triangulating. A child learning their first language is in exactly the situation you describe. No shared language, no dictionary, and yet they crack it. Not because they're smart about words, but because they're brilliant about context and intent.

And there's a deeper point here. I'd argue we never fully have a shared language. When you say "freedom" and I say "freedom," we're pointing at overlapping but different things in our heads. The gap between us is just smaller than the gap with a stranger from another country. So interpreting someone with no shared language is not a special case. It's the normal case, just turned up to eleven. The whole game of communication is me building a model of what's going on in your head, and testing it, and updating it. The word is just the hint that lets me start.

r001.rationale: The response says context such as pointing and what happens around a word can suggest several possible meanings, and its cup example explicitly keeps multiple hypotheses alive. This communicates that a pointing cue alone does not uniquely establish a word’s meaning.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to start with the context. If I say a word you’ve never heard and point at a cup, you might think, “Okay, that word means cup.” But maybe I mean water. Maybe I mean drink, or “Give that to me.” A single example doesn’t tell you which interpretation is right.

So you watch what happens when I use it again. What stays the same? What changes? You build a hypothesis, and then you test it—perhaps you hand me the cup and see how I respond. Meaning starts to emerge through that interaction. You don’t need a shared language to begin, but you do need some shared experience.

r001.rationale: The response uses a cup example instead of a rabbit, but clearly explains that pointing at an object while saying an unfamiliar word does not establish which meaning the speaker intends.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if we have no shared language, the word alone doesn’t give me very much. I have to look at the context: what you’re pointing at, what you’re doing, what happens after you say it. And then I form a hypothesis and see whether it holds the next time.

Say you point at a rabbit and say something I’ve never heard before. You might mean “rabbit,” but you might mean “look,” or “food,” or “it’s running.” One encounter doesn’t tell me which. So understanding comes from repeated interactions, where I can gradually narrow down what you might mean. Initially, I’m interpreting the whole situation, and only gradually attaching meaning to the word.

r001.rationale: The response says a word spoken while pointing at a rabbit could mean “rabbit,” “look,” “food,” or “it’s running,” so the encounter does not uniquely establish its meaning.
